overview.title: 📖 Overview: Two Chapters End, a New One Begins
overview.subtitle: Meilah 10a–10b
overview.hebrewSource: כׇּל שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ מַתִּירִין – אֵין חַיָּיבִין עָלָיו מִשּׁוּם פִּיגּוּל וְנוֹתָר וְטָמֵא עַד שֶׁיַּקְרִיבוּ מַתִּירִין
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf closes out the second chapter with two rulings from Rava — one exempting benefit derived from meat or portions that can no longer be brought to the altar (since nothing is lost from a Temple perspective), and one refining exactly when misused sin/guilt-offering money goes to the Dead Sea versus to communal gifts. A new mishna then opens the third chapter, listing items that are entirely for the altar — the handful, frankincense, incense, and special meal offerings — and introduces the crucial concept of matirin, 'permitting factors': some items need another item sacrificed first before piggul, notar, or tamei liability can apply to them. The daf ends with the opening of yet another chapter, listing the five sin offerings that must be left to die.

slides.title: 🚫 Rava's Two Refinements
slides.subtitle: Closing out the debates from recent dafim
slides.hebrewSource: הַכֹּל מוֹדִים שֶׁאִם נֶהֱנָה מִבְּשַׂר קׇדְשֵׁי קָדָשִׁים שֶׁנִּטְמָא קוֹדֶם זְרִיקָה... דְּפָטוּר
slides.label: Two rulings:
slides.text: First: everyone agrees that deriving benefit from sacred-order meat that became impure before sprinkling, or from lesser-sanctity portions already placed on the altar, incurs NO me'ilah — even though a mitzva (burning, or turning with a fork) technically remains, that mitzva is not part of the sacrificial service itself, so nothing of value is lost. Second: the earlier rule that misused sin-offering money goes to the Dead Sea applies only when the misuse became known before atonement was achieved; if it became known only after, the money goes to communal gifts instead, since 'one does not set aside money from the start intending it to be lost.'

callout.label: All share:
callout.text: Me'ilah applies from the moment of verbal consecration; susceptibility to disqualification (tevul yom, mechusar kippurim, linah) begins once placed in a vessel.

slides.title: 🔑 Deriving the Rule for Tamei From Piggul
slides.subtitle: A kal vaḥomer, then a verse, then a homiletical reading

steps.content: 1️⃣ Known: for PIGGUL, one is liable only for an item with matirin (permitting factors) — even though piggul is a strict prohibition (one awareness suffices, fixed offering, never permitted communally)
2️⃣ Kal vaḥomer: TUMAH is more lenient in structure (needs two awarenesses, sliding-scale offering, sometimes permitted communally) — so it should ALSO require matirin, if anything more so
3️⃣ But the Torah states broadly: 'anyone who approaches the sacred items... while his impurity is on him' (Leviticus 22:3) — applying to ALL sacred items, matirin or not

4️⃣ Rabbi Elazar's resolution: the odd word 'approaches' (יקרב) is read as 'fit to be offered' (יִקָּרֵב) — items WITH matirin: liable once matirin are sacrificed; items WITHOUT matirin: liable once sanctified in a vessel

callout.label: Why the verse seemed puzzling:
callout.text: A plain reading would make one liable merely for TOUCHING consecrated food — an impossible halakha, since Rabbi Elazar notes there is no such liability for touching alone.

slides.title: 🔑 With Matirin vs. Without Matirin
slides.subtitle: Two categories, two different triggers for piggul/notar/tamei liability

boxes.title: Has Matirin (e.g. meat with blood sprinkling)
items: Needs another item (like blood) sacrificed to permit it
No piggul/notar/tamei liability until the matirin are actually sacrificed

boxes.title: Has No Matirin (e.g. komeitz, levonah)
items: The item itself IS what permits others (e.g. the handful permits the remainder of a meal offering)
Notar and tamei liability begin as soon as it is sanctified in a vessel
But NO piggul liability — since piggul requires a valid act that itself creates the disqualification, and here there's no separate matir-act to misapply intent to

slides.title: 💀 New Perek: The Five Sin Offerings Left to Die
slides.subtitle: Sin offerings that may never be sacrificed and must simply be left to perish
rows: Offspring of a sin offering (וְלַד חַטָּאת)
Born from an animal already consecrated as a sin offering — has no valid use of its own
Substitute for a sin offering (תְּמוּרַת חַטָּאת)
An animal exchanged for a consecrated sin offering — inherits sanctity but not fitness for the altar
Sin offering whose owner died before it was sacrificed
No one remains to be atoned for by it
Sin offering whose year (for sacrifice) has passed
Aged past the point of validity
Sin offering lost, then found blemished — after the owner already achieved atonement elsewhere
No longer needed and now also physically unfit; does not create a substitute, and no benefit/misuse liability attaches to it

summary.principle: Me'ilah tracks genuine loss to the Temple, not mere formal steps still owed; and the concept of matirin — a permitting factor — governs exactly when piggul, notar, and tamei liability begin for items that are entirely for the altar, distinguishing them sharply from the five categories of sin offering that can never be sacrificed at all.

flowSteps.content: 🚫 No me'ilah where nothing is truly lost — impure meat before sprinkling, portions already on the altar
🌊 Misused sin-offering money: Dead Sea if known before atonement, communal gifts if known after
🕯️ New mishna: komeitz, levonah, ketoret, special meal offerings — me'ilah from consecration, notar/tamei from vessel, no piggul

columns.content: 🔑 Items WITH matirin: no liability until the permitting factor is sacrificed
🔑 Items WITHOUT matirin: liability from the moment of sanctification in a vessel

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: piggul always needs a matir; notar and tamei apply more broadly, but still track when an item is truly 'ready' for its purpose

quiz.q: According to Rava, why is one exempt from me'ilah for benefiting from sacred-order meat that became impure before sprinkling, or from lesser-sanctity portions already placed on the altar?
o: Because such meat was never actually consecrated
Because although a remaining mitzva (burning, turning) is owed, it is not part of the sacrificial service, so nothing of Temple value is truly lost
Because impure meat is never subject to any halakhot
Because the priests forfeit their rights to it
quiz.e: Rava explains that even though there's technically a mitzva left to perform (burning or turning with a fork), that act isn't part of the Temple service proper, so no real loss occurs and there's no me'ilah.

quiz.q: When does misused sin-offering money go to the Dead Sea rather than to communal gift offerings?
o: Always, regardless of timing
Only if the misuse became known before the animal was sacrificed and atonement achieved; if known afterward, it goes to communal gifts
Only if the misuse became known after atonement
Never — it always goes to communal gifts
quiz.e: Rava clarifies that Dead Sea disposal applies only when the person could still have added the money to purchase a better offering (i.e., before atonement); afterward, since one doesn't set aside money intending its loss, it goes to communal gifts.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, what liability applies to the handful (komeitz) and frankincense once they are sanctified in a service vessel?
o: Piggul, notar, and tamei liability all apply immediately
Notar and tamei liability apply, but NOT piggul liability
Only piggul liability applies
No liability of any kind applies until they are burned
quiz.e: The mishna states that items without matirin, like the handful and frankincense, incur notar and tamei liability once sanctified in a vessel, but piggul liability does not apply to them.

quiz.q: What does the concept of matirin (permitting factors) determine?
o: Which animals may be used for sacrifices
When piggul, notar, and tamei liability begin — items with matirin need the permitting factor sacrificed first; items without matirin become liable once sanctified in a vessel
The price of a sin offering
Which priests may perform the sacrificial service
quiz.e: Matirin are permitting factors (like blood sprinkling) that must be sacrificed before an item becomes subject to piggul/notar/tamei; items that lack matirin (like the handful itself) become liable simply upon being sanctified in a vessel.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five sin offerings left to die according to the new mishna?
o: The offspring of a sin offering
A sin offering whose owner died before it was sacrificed
A sin offering that was properly sacrificed and eaten by the priests
A sin offering found blemished after the owner already achieved atonement with another animal
quiz.e: A properly sacrificed and eaten sin offering is not one of the five left-to-die categories; the five are the offspring, the substitute, one whose owner died, one whose year has passed, and one lost-then-found-blemished after atonement.
